fields.question: What can content-routed MoBA recover that a recent window cannot?
fields.answer: A window excludes positions by age. Routing can recover relevant distant blocks but can still miss evidence. Cost depends on block size and routing budget; it is not lossless pruning.
fields.example: A name at the beginning can return through content matching instead of being automatically excluded.

fields.question: Does selecting the current MoBA block remove the need for causality inside it?
fields.answer: No. Mask positions after the query inside the selected block. The local eight-token, top-two configuration is not a million-context fused kernel.
fields.example: Word three cannot read word seven merely because both share an eight-token block.

fields.question: How does Möbius position encoding differ from standard RoPE across a training window?
fields.answer: Antiperiodic frequencies on some heads yield −I at one window and I at two. Other heads retain standard RoPE for language modeling. This changes positional geometry, not accessible history or guaranteed retrieval at all lengths.
fields.example: At N positions the selected heads reverse phase; at 2N they realign. Actual retrieval still depends on Q/K and training.

fields.question: What retrieval instability is Möbius RoPE intended to address?
fields.answer: Standard RoPE long-range needle retrieval can vary strongly by training seed. Antiperiodic frequencies on some heads aim to stabilize cross-window phase while leaving others unchanged.
fields.example: Identical needles in long text can produce very different retrieval results across seeds.

fields.question: What explicit frequency boundary does Möbius add?
fields.answer: Set some two-dimensional frequencies to π(2i+1)/N, producing −I across N and I across 2N. Other heads keep standard RoPE. This is geometry, not measured improvement.
fields.example: Reverse phase after one window and recover after two, not arbitrary scaling across every head.

fields.question: Should Möbius RoPE change N dynamically with inference length?
fields.answer: No. N is fixed training context; local N=64 replaces one of four heads. Dynamic N changes frequencies for identical positions and breaks the boundary definition. Retain negative local results.
fields.example: Length-32 and length-80 inputs both use the same training N.

fields.question: How does MS-GLA avoid leaking later tokens when pooling a block?
fields.answer: Each coarse branch masked-averages nonoverlapping blocks and runs GLA. A summary becomes visible only at the block end; causal hold restores token resolution without broadcasting into earlier positions. Input-conditioned weights fuse scales.
fields.example: In a four-token block, position two cannot see the average including positions three and four.

fields.question: Why give MS-GLA heads different temporal scales?
fields.answer: One resolution can bottleneck representations. Some heads preserve token-level variation, others use pooled history, and their outputs combine.
fields.example: Phrase detail and trends across phrases can use different update rates.

fields.question: Why is multiscale GLA more than a larger window?
fields.answer: Each scale pools at a different nonoverlapping granularity before GLA, changing temporal update resolution. Extending a window still updates at the original rate.
fields.example: Updating once per four words differs from updating every word while looking farther back.

fields.question: When may tokens access scale-four pooled state?
fields.answer: At or after the block's final token. Use causal hold and input softmax fusion rather than broadcasting full means to every token.
fields.example: Token one cannot use the average of words one through four before word four arrives.

fields.question: Why separate retention and writing rather than use complementary gates in Naju?
fields.answer: A complementary write would shrink whenever retention is strong. Independent gates on native discrete dynamics can preserve old state and write new evidence together. Token-dependent directions, convolution, and feedthrough still matter.
fields.example: Keep a name while adding age instead of erasing the name in proportion to the new write.

fields.question: Why independently control old-state retention and new writes?
fields.answer: A shared complementary gate creates a tradeoff. Separate retain/write gates in the discrete transition let both adjust independently.
fields.example: Reading an important new fact need not erase an old fact.

fields.question: How do Naju's native discrete poles differ from Mamba discretizing continuous dynamics?
fields.answer: Naju directly parameterizes discrete retention. Mamba derives a transition from continuous dynamics and input-dependent time steps. Both recur but formulas and gate coupling differ.
fields.example: One learns the retained fraction per step directly; the other derives it from a time step and continuous matrix.

fields.question: How should preserve-first initialization set Naju's two gates?
fields.answer: forget_bias=5 and write_bias=−2 create strong initial retention and weak writes. Retain token-dependent B/C and direct feedthrough.
fields.example: Sigmoid(5)≈0.993 and sigmoid(−2)≈0.119 are not equal gates.

fields.question: Why retain original blocks and a sliding window in addition to compressed NSA history?
fields.answer: Compression gives cheap global context but can lose details. Query-selected original blocks recover precise evidence, and a window covers recent tokens. All three paths learn and fuse from pretraining and remain causal.
fields.example: A summary can identify the chapter about dates; exact selected tokens resolve the year and the window preserves current qualifiers.

fields.question: Why use compression, selection, and window paths together?
fields.answer: They provide global overview, exact selected detail, and exact recent context, respectively. Learned gates combine them; one sparsity pattern need not serve all roles.
fields.example: Get topic summary, a distant key sentence, and current phrase detail from different paths.

fields.question: How does NSA differ from pruning low attention weights after training?
fields.answer: Three paths and their gates are trained jointly from pretraining, changing what the model learns to access. Post-hoc deletion from a dense model does not provide the same adaptation.
fields.example: The model learns to trade summary and detailed blocks rather than suddenly losing history.

fields.question: Do all three NSA branches need causal boundaries?
fields.answer: Yes. Compressed blocks, selected fine blocks, and windows cannot expose future information. Align output dimensions before gated fusion. Local edge counts do not measure paper Triton throughput.
fields.example: Mask future words in a selected block spanning the query position.

fields.question: Why group QK contribution dimensions and calibrate OAL against output error?
fields.answer: A few coordinates can dominate softmax approximation error. OAL finds stable post-RoPE groups and learns positive-definite quadratic kernels for shared groups and pairs. Vectors after aggregation, not only weights, reveal impact; positivity protects normalization.
fields.example: Equal weight errors have different effects if one location has a large or very different value.

fields.question: Why focus on high-contribution post-RoPE QK coordinates?
fields.answer: Coordinate contributions are uneven; a high-contribution tail can dominate error. Grouping and positive quadratic kernels target these differences rather than treating every coordinate alike.
fields.example: A few coordinates driving most score changes merit different approximation from low-contribution ones.

fields.question: How does OAL output MSE differ from fitting attention weights?
fields.answer: Output depends on values and normalized aggregation, so equal weight errors can affect outputs differently. Calibrate the kernel to actual readouts.
fields.example: Swapping weights on identical values changes nothing, unlike swapping opposite values.

fields.question: Which OAL grouping, calibration, and initialization choices may use test data?
fields.answer: None. Train supports grouping, calibration, and LoRA; validation selects initialization and checkpoint; test comes last. Keep ε in the positive kernel to ensure a positive denominator.
fields.example: Do not replace the validation-selected kernel with one found better on test and report that same test again.

fields.question: When does On-Demand Attention trigger global retrieval?
fields.answer: A cheap recall head predicts benefit before expensive global attention and triggers it only for worthwhile tokens. Full KV stays stored; it saves some reads, not cache capacity. Misses can hide relevant distant evidence.
fields.example: Punctuation may use local context, while quoting an opening number triggers global reading; decide before paying for it.

fields.question: Are ODA local and remote history divided by importance?
fields.answer: No. They describe distance relative to the current token. Relevant evidence can be far and nearby words irrelevant, motivating optional global reads.
fields.example: A name at the document start can be critical outside the current window.

fields.question: How does on-demand retrieval differ from evicting old KV?
fields.answer: ODA retains all KV and varies when it is read. Eviction removes historical entries from the accessible set and changes memory capacity as well.
fields.example: A token skipped now may still be retrieved next step if retained.
